code.title: Where value types live: copies vs shared objects

followUps:
When the value is only used inside the method, the JIT's escape analysis can prove that the object never leaves it, so it can place the object on the stack instead of the heap. .NET 9 added this for simple cases, and .NET 10 extended it.

For example, var p = new Point(1, 2); return p.X + p.Y; allocates nothing because p is never stored in a field, returned, passed to something unknown, or captured. It is an optimisation, not a language guarantee, so do not rely on it for correctness.

code.title: Boxing makes a heap copy

followUps:
Look for the allocations, because every box is one. Measure first, then find the sites.

  1. Run dotnet-counters and watch the allocation rate and gen 0 GC count.
  2. Use an allocation profiler or dotnet-trace and look for System.Int32 or your struct type being allocated as an object.
  3. Read the IL for box instructions.
  4. Write a BenchmarkDotNet test with [MemoryDiagnoser]: the Allocated column must be 0 B after the fix.

Example: 1,000,000 boxed ints is about 24 MB of garbage.

code.title: Short-lived objects die at the next collection

followUps:
It is a young-looking object that survives gen 0 and gen 1 collections and then dies soon after in gen 2, where it costs far more to clean up. Cache entries and objects held for a few seconds are typical.

Each survival means the GC copies the object during compaction, and each gen 2 collection scans a big heap. Example: a request object lives 200 ms and gets promoted to gen 2 by two collections in that time; then it dies, and only a full collection frees it. Fixes: keep objects shorter-lived than a GC cycle, or deliberately long-lived (pools), and reduce the allocation rate.

Workstation GC is tuned for low latency on a desktop or small app, and server GC is tuned for throughput on many cores. Server GC creates one heap and one dedicated GC thread per logical core, uses bigger gen 0 budgets, and collects in parallel, so it uses more memory but pauses less per allocated byte.

Example: a web API on 16 cores usually picks server GC (<ServerGarbageCollector>true</ServerGarbageCollector>); a UI app keeps workstation GC. In containers with a small CPU limit, workstation is often better. Measure both.

code.title: LOH threshold and List growth

followUps:
Its internal array doubles when it is full, and once that array reaches 85,000 bytes it is allocated on the LOH. Each further doubling allocates a bigger LOH array and abandons the old one.

For a List<int> the limit is 21,250 elements (4 bytes each), so growth to capacity 32,768 allocates 131,072 bytes on the LOH. A List<object> hits it at about 10,625 elements on 64-bit. Avoid it by giving the expected size: new List<int>(50000) allocates once instead of several times.

code.title: Dispose vs finalizer

followUps:
Dispose(bool disposing) is one method that handles both cleanup paths, so the same code is not copied into Dispose() and the finalizer.

public void Dispose() { Dispose(true); GC.SuppressFinalize(this); }
protected virtual void Dispose(bool disposing) {
  if (disposed) return; disposed = true;
  if (disposing) { other.Dispose(); }   // managed
  CloseHandle(raw);                     // unmanaged
}
~C() { Dispose(false); }

The flag is true when the owner calls it and false from the finalizer; the guard makes a second call harmless.

code.title: Dispose(bool disposing) paths

followUps:
A SafeHandle is a ready-made wrapper that owns an operating system handle and already contains a correct finalizer, so your class needs none of its own.

It is preferred because it is reference counted during P/Invoke calls (the handle cannot be closed while a native call is using it), it is reliably released even if the thread is aborted or the process is low on memory, and it prevents handle recycling attacks. Example: FileStream holds a SafeFileHandle; if you forget to dispose the stream, the handle still closes. Your class then only implements Dispose and never touches the finalizer.

code.title: Span slicing without copying

followUps:
A ref struct cannot ever be moved to the heap, because it may hold a reference to stack memory. The compiler enforces that.

  • It cannot be a field of a class or of a normal struct.
  • It cannot be boxed, so it cannot be cast to object or an interface (before C# 13).
  • It cannot be captured by a lambda or local function.
  • It cannot be a local in an async method or an iterator, or used across await/yield.
  • It cannot be a generic argument (before C# 13).

Use Memory<T> when you hit one of these limits.

code.title: Memory<T> across await

followUps:
MemoryManager<T> lets you create a Memory<T> over memory that is not a managed array, such as native memory or a memory-mapped file, and control how it is pinned and released.

You derive from it and implement GetSpan(), Pin(), Unpin() and Dispose. After that, manager.Memory flows through any API that takes Memory<byte>, for example socket reads. ArrayPool and the Kestrel buffer pool use this mechanism to hand out memory with an owner that returns it when disposed.

It changes the compiler so it does not zero the memory of locals and of stackalloc blocks, which saves time but leaves old garbage in the memory.

Normally the runtime sets all locals to 0 on method entry (the .locals init flag). With [SkipLocalsInit] a stackalloc byte[1024] starts with whatever was on the stack. It needs unsafe code enabled. It is a real gain for large stackalloc buffers you fill yourself, but reading before writing gives random data and can leak secrets, so only use it when you overwrite every byte first.

code.title: ArrayPool rent, return and stale reference

followUps:
Pooling is slower or not worth it when the arrays are small or short-lived, because a small gen 0 allocation is just a pointer bump and is cheap to collect.

Renting costs a bucket lookup, possible thread-local access, a clear on return, and bugs from stale data. Rule of thumb: pool arrays larger than about 1 KB that are allocated often, especially near the 85,000 byte LOH limit. For a 64-byte array in a request path, new byte[64] usually wins, and a stack buffer is better still. Always measure with BenchmarkDotNet before adding a pool.

A GC root is a reference the GC treats as always alive, and everything reachable from a root cannot be collected. This is why a leak is always a path from a root to the object.

Roots are: static fields, local variables and parameters on thread stacks (and registers), GC handles (including pinned and strong handles), and the finalization queue. Example leak: a static Dictionary cache with no eviction holds every entry forever; an event handler on a long-lived publisher roots the subscriber. In a heap dump you follow the "gcroot" path to find which of these holds the object.

code.title: Struct array vs object array memory

followUps:
A struct becomes slower when it is large or copied a lot, because every assignment, argument pass and return copies all its bytes, while a class only copies an 8-byte reference.

Example: a 64-byte struct passed through five method calls copies 320 bytes, but a class passes 40 bytes of references. Boxing also adds cost. Rule of thumb: keep a struct to about 16 bytes, make it immutable, and pass larger ones by in or ref. Sorting an array of big structs also moves more data per swap than sorting references.

code.title: Modifying a struct inside a List

followUps:
A ref return gives you a reference to the actual storage instead of a copy, so you can change the element in place.

An array indexer already behaves like that. For a list, ref var p = ref CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list)[i]; p.X = 1; modifies the list's real element. Or you can write your own method ref P At(int i) => ref items[i]; and call At(3).X = 9;. The warning: if the list grows and reallocates, an old ref points at the abandoned array, so use it briefly and never add items while holding it.

code.title: Nulling a field helps, locals do not

followUps:
GC.KeepAlive(obj) does nothing at run time; it is a marker that says the object must be treated as in use up to that point, so the GC cannot collect it earlier.

It matters when only unmanaged code holds a resource of the object. Example: you pass obj.Handle (a raw integer) to a native call, and the JIT sees obj as unused after reading the handle; the GC could finalize obj and close the handle during the call. Putting GC.KeepAlive(obj); after the native call prevents that. It is also used in benchmarks so the work is not optimised away.
